newsitem.title: FRANCE: French police swoop on Moslems after bombing.
newsitem.headline: French police swoop on Moslems after bombing.

text.p: French police swooped on suspected Moslem militants on Tuesday, rounding up 15 people in dawn raids across Paris a week after the bombing of a city train which killed four people.

Police and counter-espionage officers searched buildings housing Moslems in Paris and the suburbs on orders from anti-terrorism magistrates who are investigating 1995 bombings by Algerian Moslem extremists that killed eight people and injured more than 160.
Police said the swoops were not directly linked to last Tuesday's attack at the capital's Port-Royal station which bore the hallmarks of Algerian Moslem extremists.

Investigators said the raids targeted a network allegedly run by Ahmed Zaoui, former European leader of Algeria's Islamic Armed Group (GIA). He was given a suspended four-year jail sentence by a Belgian court in November 1995.
The network, based in Chasse-sur-Rhone outside Lyon in central France, was one of three partly dismantled by French authorities after the 1995 bombings.
"France has again been hit by terrorism...The French people will once again remain calm and show courage and solidarity," President Jacques Chirac told a national human rights watchdog.
"We will not let certain groups enslave souls and destroy free choice by hiding behind freedom of faith," he said.

Searches were carried out in the Essone department south of Paris, where a 13 kg (28lb) gas canister similar to that used in the train bombing was detonated in Saint-Maurice Montcouronne on the night of November 19, shattering a roadman's shed in what may have been a test of the device.

In Paris, some of the 34 Moslem fundamentalists on trial accused of supporting Moroccan guerrillas denounced the men they are charged with backing -- Mohamed "Said" Zinedine and Abdelilah "Rachid" Ziyad.

"Said had ordered a pact with God. We had to promise not to go back, to go forward until death. If someone went back, the others were supposed to shoot him," testified Tarek Falah, 22, who has admitted taking part in the killing of two Spanish tourists in Marrakech in August 1994.
"I was only a puppet," said Tarek's brother Rachid, 30. "My brother Tarek was hypnotised by Said who never let him go. He had found cannon-fodder."

Prosecutors say the Moroccans were recruited in Paris and other cities, given guerrilla training in camps in Afghanistan and Algeria, and religiously indoctrinated before being sent on missions to North Africa, many of which were botched.
Investigators believe the Paris train bomb may have been timed to protest at the trial.

No one has claimed responsibility for the rush-hour train bombing, which killed four people and injured 94. It bore similarities to last year's bombing wave, which ended after dozens of suspects were rounded up in raids around France.

Chirac, in a letter of condoleances to Moroccan King Hassan after Moroccan student Younes Nait-Slimane became the fourth victim of the train blast on Monday, pledged "to fight terrorism, this plague which threatens democracy".

Roland Jacquard, head of the International Observatory of Terrorism, said Tuesday's raids seemed partly aimed at tracking down people with links to Ali Touchent, one of the main Algerian suspects in last year's bombings, who is still free.
